Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verses 1–2:

﴿A revelation of the Book from Allah﴾. ﴿Tanzil (revelation)﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿from Allah﴾. Or its predicate is an omitted beginning (ibtida') whose implied meaning is: "This is a revelation." On this reading, ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to "revelation," or it is a predicate following a predicate, or the predicate of another omitted subject. ﴿The Book﴾ here refers to the Qur'an, or to the surah. Ibn 'Atiyya chose that it refers to the genus of revealed books. As for the second "Book," it is the Qur'an by consensus. ﴿With truth﴾ may carry two meanings: first, that its meaning includes truth; second, that its meaning is by right and necessity. ﴿Making the religion sincerely His﴾. It is said: its meaning is that it is incumbent upon him and his duty that the pure religion be His alone. It may also mean: the pure religion is the religion of Allah, which is Islam, which He prescribed for His servants and does not accept other than it. The meaning of "pure" (khalis) is what is free from the impurities of polytheism. Qatada said: the pure religion is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. Al-Hasan said: it is Islam. This is the more preponderant view because of its generality.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 3:

﴿Those who take protectors besides Him﴾. By "protectors" (awliya') he means the associate deities that are worshipped. It is also possible that he means by "those who took" the disbelievers who worship them, or the associate deities that are worshipped. The first is more apparent, because the second requires omitting the pronoun referring back to "those who" (alladhina), whose full form would be "those who took them" (alladhina ittakhadhuhum). The subject pronoun in "took" (ittakhadhu) would then refer to something not previously mentioned. On both readings, "those who" (alladhina) is in the nominative as the inceptive subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject beginning a nominal sentence). Its predicate (khabar) is either His words ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾, or the omitted element assumed before His words ﴿We only worship them﴾, since its full form would be "they say: we only worship them." The first is more preferred, because its meaning is more complete.

﴿We only worship them except that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾. This clause is in the position of the object (ma'mul, the complement) of an omitted verb of saying. The saying itself is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) or in the position of a substitute (badal) for the relative clause (silat) of "those who." Ibn Mas'ud read "they said: we do not worship them," with the verb of saying made explicit. The meaning is: the disbelievers say, "We do not worship these deities except that they bring us near to Allah and intercede for us with Him." By this is meant the disbelievers who worshipped the angels, or those who worshipped idols, or those who worshipped Jesus or Ezra, for all of them made this same statement.

The word "in position" (zulfa) means nearness (qurba). It is a verbal noun (masdar) from "they bring us near" (yuqarribuna).

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and a stubborn disbeliever﴾. This refers to the falsity of their claim, "they bring us near to Allah," and His words "does not guide" have two interpretations. The first: He does not guide him while he remains in his disbelief. The second: this applies specifically to one whom Allah has decreed to die upon disbelief. May Allah protect us from that. This is to be understood as: "Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people (al-qawm al-zalimin) and the disbelieving people (al-kafirin)" wherever it occurs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 4:

﴿Had Allah wished to take a son, He would have chosen whomever He willed from among what He creates.﴾ Walad (son, offspring) occurs in two senses. The first is begetting in the true sense, and this is impossible for Allah, the Exalted; it is not permissible by reason. The second is adoption, in the sense of special favour and closeness, as a person takes another's child as his own son out of excessive love for him. This is impossible for Allah by the report of the Sharia, for His saying: ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful that He should take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92] encompasses the negation of both senses. So the meaning of the verse, as Ibn 'Atiyya indicated, is: Had Allah wished to take a son by way of adoption, He would have chosen for that purpose from among His existing and created beings. But He did not wish that, nor did He do it. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that if Allah wished to take a son, that would be prevented; but He chooses from among His servants whomever He wills, by way of special favour and closeness, not by way of taking them as sons. Thus He chose the angels and honoured them with closeness, so the disbelievers supposed that they were His offspring, and then they went further and made them females, exceeding in disbelief and in lying against Allah and His angels.

﴿Glory be to Him! He is Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, declared Himself far exalted above taking a son. Then He described Himself as "the One" (al-Wahid), because oneness (al-wahdaniyya) is incompatible with taking a son: for if He had a son, the son would be of His kind, and He has no kind, since He is One. He described Himself as "the Subduer" (al-Qahhar) to indicate the negation of partners and equals, for every thing is subdued under His dominion, so how could it be a partner to Him? Then He followed this with what He mentioned of the creation of the heavens and the earth and what lies between them, to indicate His oneness, His power, and His greatness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 5:

﴿He wraps the night over the day﴾ At-Takwir (تكوير) means wrapping and winding around, and from it comes "kawwara al-'imamah" (he wound the turban), where one part of it coils over another. Here it is a metaphor (isti'arah). Its meaning, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, is that one of them renews (يعيد) its course over the other: so the one that lengthens, whether the day or the night, takes a portion of the other upon itself and covers it, and the one that shortens enters into the one that lengthens and is concealed within it. It is also possible that the meaning is that each of them overcomes the other when it comes upon it, and so its covering of the other is likened to a garment wound around something. ﴿for a term appointed﴾ means the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 6:

﴿He created you from a single soul﴾, meaning Adam (peace be upon him). ﴿Then He made from it its mate﴾, meaning Hawwa' (Eve), whom He created from a rib of Adam. If it is said: how is His saying ﴿then He made﴾ conjoined to "created you" with "thumma" (then), which requires sequence and an interval, when there is no doubt that the creation of Hawwa' was before the creation of the children of Adam? The answer is in three aspects. The first, which is the preferred one, is that the conjunction is only upon the meaning of His saying ﴿single﴾, not upon "created you", as if He said: He created you from a soul that was single, then He created from it its mate after its singleness. The second: "thumma" here is for sequence of reporting, not for sequence of existence. The third: by His saying ﴿created you﴾ He means the bringing forth of the children of Adam from the loins of their father like the particles (dharr), and that was before the creation of Hawwa'.

﴿And He sent down for you of the grazing animals eight mates﴾, meaning those mentioned in the chapter of al-An'am: two from the sheep, two from the goats, and two from the cattle. He called them "mates" (azwaj) because the male is a mate of the female and the female is a mate of the male. As for ﴿sent down﴾ (anzala), there are three aspects to it. The first: that God created the first of these pairs in the heaven and then sent them down. The second: that the meaning of "sent down" is "decreed and apportioned", so the sending down is an expression for the descent of His command and decree. The third: that He sent down the rain by which plants grow, on which these livestock live, and so He expressed the sending down of them for the sending down of their provisions; and this is far-fetched. ﴿Creation after creation﴾, meaning that the human being becomes a drop (nutfah), then a clot ( 'alaqah), then a lump of flesh (mudghah), until his creation is complete, then the spirit is breathed into him. ﴿In three darknesses﴾: they are the belly, the womb, and the placenta (mashimah). It was said: the loins of the father, the womb, and the placenta; and the first is more preferred because of His saying ﴿in the bellies of your mothers﴾, and He did not mention the loins.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 7:

﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need from you﴾, meaning: your disbelief does not harm Him.

﴿And He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾. The Ash'arites (al-Ash'ariyya) interpret this verse in two ways. The first is that approval (al-rida) means will (al-iradah), and by "His servants" is meant those for whom Allah has decreed faith and that they die in it. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42; al-Isra': 65]. The second is that approval is other than will, and "the servants" here is general, meaning that He does not approve disbelief for any of mankind. Even though He willed that it occur from some of them, He did not approve it as religion or as law, and He willed it to occur and to exist. As for the Mu'tazilites (al-Mu'tazila), approval for them means will, and "the servants" in this case is general, in keeping with their principle regarding predestination (al-qadar) and the acts of servants.

﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾. This is general, and true gratitude includes faith.

﴿No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. This was mentioned in al-Isra'.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 8:

﴿And when harm touches man﴾ etc.: By "man" (al-insan) here is meant the disbeliever, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and sets up rivals to God﴾. The aim of this verse is rebuke and the establishment of proof: the rebuke is for disbelief and for abandoning the supplication of God, and the proof is established against the human being by calling him to God in times of hardship. If it is asked: why does He say here ﴿And when﴾ with a waw, and after it say ﴿So when﴾ [az-Zumar: 49] with a fa'? The answer: the one with fa' is a consequence of His saying: ﴿the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink﴾ [az-Zumar: 45], so it comes with the fa' of causation; this is what az-Zamakhshari said, but it is far-fetched.

﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favour from Himself﴾: khawwalahu means He gave him (a'taahu). The favour here may be understood as the removal of the harm mentioned, or any favour whatsoever. ﴿he forgets what he was calling upon Him for before﴾: it may be that ma is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), meaning he forgets his supplication; or it may be in the sense of alladhi (that which), and what is meant is God, exalted is He.

﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient﴾ is read with the mim lightened, placing the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham) before man (من). It was also said that it is the hamza of address (hamzat al-nida'), but the first view is more apparent. It was also recited with the mim doubled, placing umm (أم) before man (من). Man is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted. It is the mu'adil (the counterpart that balances the question), and its estimated form is: أم من هو قانت كغيره (or is one who is devoutly obedient like the other?). It was omitted because the context indicates it, namely what was mentioned before it and what was mentioned after it, which is his saying: ﴿Are those who know equal?﴾ Qunut (devout obedience) here means obedience and prayer at night, and anaa' al-layl (آناء الليل) means its hours.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 10:

﴿O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good,﴾ and so on. The verse was revealed concerning Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and his companions when they resolved to emigrate (hijra) to the land of Habasha (Abyssinia). Its meaning is to comfort them and encourage them to emigrate. ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good.﴾ It may be that "in this world" is connected to "did good," so the meaning is: those who did good in the world have good in the Hereafter. Or it may be connected to "good," and "good" in this case means a good condition and well-being in this world. The first is more preferred. ﴿And God's earth is spacious.﴾ This refers to the lands neighbouring the land from which they emigrated, and the purpose of this is to urge them to emigrate.

﴿Only the patient will be given their reward without reckoning.﴾ This has two possible meanings. The first is that the patient one is given his reward and is not called to account for his deeds, so he is among those who enter Paradise without reckoning. The second is that the reward of the patient is without limit, rather it is more than can be confined by number or measure, and this is the view of the majority (al-jumhur).

"And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims." The lam here may be extra (zā'idah, emphatic) or for causation (li-ta'līl), and the object (al-maf'ūl) is then omitted. If it is asked: how is "umirtu" conjoined to "umirtu" when the meaning is the same? The answer is that the first is a command to worship and to sincerity (ikhlāṣ), and the second is a command to precede in Islam; so they are two distinct meanings. Likewise His saying: ﴿Say: It is God I worship﴾ is not a repetition of His saying ﴿I have been commanded to worship God﴾, because the first is a report that he is commanded to worship, and the second is a report that he is performing the worship. The name of God, exalted is He, is placed first for restriction (al-ḥaṣr) and for the exclusivity of worship to Him alone. ﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾: this is a threat and an intensification of their abandonment (khudhlān), and a leaving of them to what they are upon. ﴿Ẓulal﴾ is the plural of ẓullah (with a ḍammah), which is that which covers from above like a roof; so His saying ﴿from above them﴾ is clear. As for ﴿and from beneath them﴾, He called it ẓullah because it is a roof for those beneath them, since Hell has layers. It is also said: He called it ẓullah because it blazes and rises from below them up to above them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 17:

﴿And those who avoid the taghut, not worshipping them﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd, Sa'id, Talha and al-Zubayr, when Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) invited them to faith and they believed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Dharr and Salman, but this is weak, because Salman embraced Islam in Medina, whereas the verse is Meccan. The more apparent view is that it is general, and the taghut (every object of worship besides Allah) is everything that is worshipped apart from Allah. It was also said: the taghut refers to the devils (shayatin).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verses 18–19:

﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾. It has been said: they listen to speech in general and then follow the Qur'an, because it is the best of speech. It has also been said: they listen to the Qur'an and then follow its best in their deeds, such as pardoning, which is better than retaliating, and similar things. It has also been said: this refers to one who hears a statement containing both good and bad, so he speaks of the good and refrains from the rest. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the most apparent. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a general term covering all sayings. The purpose is to praise these people for their insight and sound judgment, by which they distinguish between truth and falsehood and between right and wrong, and so they follow the better of these.

Al-Zamakhshari said: this may be read as one continuous sentence, its sense being: "Is one against whom the word of punishment has been fulfilled [to be saved]? Can you rescue him who is in the Fire?" Here the phrase "man fi al-nar" (he who is in the Fire) takes the place of a pronoun, and the hamza in the words ﴿Then are you﴾ is the same hamza found in ﴿Then is he who﴾; it is the hamza of disapproval, repeated for emphasis. The second possibility is that the sense is: "Is one against whom the punishment has been fulfilled [a case for which] you grieve?", where the predicate is omitted, and then he resumes with ﴿Then are you going to rescue those in the Fire?﴾. On this reading one stops at "al-'adhab" (the punishment). The first reading is preferable because it involves no omission of a pronoun.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 21:

﴿So He made it flow as springs in the earth﴾. The meaning of "salakahu" (made it flow) is that He caused it to enter and run. Yanabi' (springs) is the plural of yanbu', which is a spring (ʿayn). This is evidence that the water of springs comes from rain. ﴿Varying in its colors﴾, meaning its kinds, such as wheat, rice, fava beans and other things. It has been said: its colors are green, red and the like. Both interpretations are evidence for the Chooser who acts by choice, and a refutation of the naturalists [the atheists].

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 39, verse 22:

﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam﴾: its implied meaning is, "Is one whose breast Allah has opened like one whose heart is hard?" It is narrated that the one whose breast Allah opened to Islam was ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Ḥamzah, and by "those whose hearts are hard" is meant Abū Lahab and his sons, though the wording is more general than that. ﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Min" here is causal, meaning "their hearts are hard because of the remembrance of Allah." But this meaning is far-fetched. In my view it is possible that "qāsiyah" (hard) is taken to include the meaning of "khāliyah" (empty), which is why it takes "min," meaning: their hearts are empty of the remembrance of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 23:

﴿ٱللَّهُ نَزَّلَ أَحْسَنَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ﴾ "Allah has sent down the best of speech," meaning the Qur'an. ﴿كِتَاباً﴾ (a Book) is either a substitute (badal) for "the best," or a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it. ﴿مُّتَشَابِهاً﴾ (uniform/similar) here means that its parts resemble one another in eloquence and in speaking the truth, and that there is in it no contradiction or discrepancy. ﴿مَّثَانِيَ﴾ (oft-repeated) is the plural of mathani, meaning that stories are repeated and recounted within it. It may also be derived from ath-thana' (praise), because praise of Allah is repeated in it. If it is asked: mathani is plural, so how is it used to describe a singular noun? The answer: the Qur'an is divided into many surahs and verses, so it is plural in this respect. It is also permissible that it be like their saying: "barmah a'shar" (a cooking pot in pieces) and "thawb akhlaq" (a worn-out garment), or that it be a specification (tamyiz) of "mutashabihan," as in your saying: "husn shama'il" (beautiful dispositions).

﴿ثُمَّ تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ "Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah." If it is asked: how is talin (soften) construed with ila (to)? The answer: it includes the meaning of a verb that takes ila, as if he said: their hearts incline, or become calm, or find rest, toward the remembrance of Allah. If it is asked: why did you mention the skins alone first, and then mention the hearts along with them afterward? The answer: when he said first "taqsha'irru" (they shudder), he mentioned the skins alone, because shuddering is a description of skins and not of anything else. When he said second "talin" (they soften), he mentioned both skins and hearts, because softness is a description applied to both skins and hearts. As for the softening of hearts, it is the opposite of their hardness; as for the softening of skins, it is the opposite of their shuddering. So they shuddered first from fear, then softened through hope.

﴿ذَلِكَ هُدَى ٱللَّهِ﴾ "That is the guidance of Allah." The reference (ishara) may be to the Qur'an, or to the awe and shuddering of the skins.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 24:

﴿Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment﴾. The predicate is omitted, as was explained in similar cases earlier; its implied sense is: "Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment like one who is secure from the punishment?" The meaning of "yattaqi" (shields, guards oneself) is that he meets the Fire with his face in order to keep it away from himself. This is because when a person encounters something frightening, he meets it with his hands, but the hands of these people are chained, so they shield themselves from the Fire with their faces. ﴿Taste what you used to earn﴾, that is, taste the requital for what you used to earn of disbelief and disobedience.

Qur'an, Arabic, (as) a Qur'an (qur'anan 'arabiyyan) — accusative, either as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) or by an implied verb in the sense of praise (ʿalā al-madḥ). ﴿Without any crookedness﴾ (ghayra dhī ʿiwaj): meaning there is no contradiction (taḍādd) or discrepancy (ikhtilāf) in it, nor any of the defects found in human speech. It is said that its meaning is: uncreated. It is also said: without any solecism (laḥn).

If it is asked: why did He say ﴿ghayra dhī ʿiwaj﴾ and not "ghayr muʿawwaj" (not crooked)? The answer: His saying ﴿ghayra dhī ʿiwaj﴾ is more emphatic in negating crookedness from it, as if He said: there is nothing of crookedness in it at all.

Verse 29 of Surah 39 (az-Zumar), Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil):

﴿A man belonging to several partners who are quarrelsome﴾ means: disputing with one another and wronging one another. It is also said: quarrelling with one another. Its root is from your saying "rajul shakis" (a man of shakis), meaning one whose chest is narrow (ill-tempered). The meaning is that this parable was coined to explain the condition of the one who associates others with God and the one who affirms His oneness. The polytheist is likened to a slave shared among a group of partners who dispute over him, and the slave among them is in the worst of states. The one who affirms God's oneness is likened to a slave belonging to one man. So His saying ﴿wholly devoted to one man﴾ means: purely his, belonging exclusively to him. It is also read as "salaman" without the alif, and the meaning is the same.

Qur'an 39:30: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die.﴾ In this is a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ) and a warning to the disbelievers, for when they all die and return to God, those who were upon the truth will succeed and those who were upon falsehood will perish. And in it also is an announcement that he (ﷺ) will die, so that people would not differ concerning his death as the nations differed concerning the death of others. It has been reported that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may God be pleased with him) denied his death, until Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may God be pleased with him) argued against him with this verse, and he returned to it.

"﴿You will dispute﴾. It has been said: it means the dispute over blood (killing). It has also been said: over rights. The more evident view is that it is the dispute of the Prophet ﷺ with the disbelievers over their denial of him, so that it is part of what precedes it. It is also possible that it is general, covering the disputing of creatures among themselves over wrongs and other matters."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 32:

﴿Who then is more unjust than one who lies against Allah﴾. The meaning: no one is more unjust than one who lies against Allah, and by lying against Allah here he means what they attributed to Him of partners and offspring. ﴿and denies the truth﴾, i.e., he denies Islam and the Sharia.

﴿And the one who brings the truth and confirms it: those are the righteous.﴾

It was said: "The one who brings the truth is the Prophet (ﷺ), and the one who confirms it is Abu Bakr." It was also said: "The one who brings the truth is Jibril (Gabriel), and the one who confirms it is Muhammad (ﷺ)." And it was said: "The one who brings the truth is the prophets, and the one who confirms it is the believers." Ibn Atiyyah chose that it be general, and he treated alladhi (the one) as referring to a category, as if he had said: "the group who," because it stands in contrast to those who lied against Allah and denied the truth, and what is meant by it is generality.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 36:

﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ This is a strengthening of the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) and a removal of the fear with which the disbelievers were threatening him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 38:

﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ The verse is an argument for tawhid (the oneness of God) and a rebuttal of the polytheists. ﴿Can they, then, remove the harm of Allah?﴾ It is a refutation of the polytheists and a proof of God's unity. It is reported that its occasion of revelation was that the polytheists frightened the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with their gods, so the verse came down clarifying that they have no power over anything. If it is asked, why is "kashifat" (removers) and "mumsikat" (withholders) in the feminine form? The answer is that they are not rational beings, so their grammatical treatment is that of feminine entities; and also, feminizing them is a belittling of them and a mockery of those who worship them.
﴿Work according to your position﴾: a threat and a token of peace, abrogated (mansukh) by the sword. ﴿Indeed I﴾ is mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 42:

﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep.﴾ This verse is a lesson (i'tibar), and its meaning is that Allah takes the souls in two ways. One: a complete, real taking, which is death. The other: the taking of sleep, because the sleeper is like the dead in that he neither sees nor hears. From this is His saying: ﴿And it is He who takes you back at night﴾ [al-An'am: 60]. Its implied meaning is: and He takes the souls that have not died during their sleep. ﴿Then He withholds those on whom He has decreed death﴾, i.e., He withholds the souls upon which He has decreed real death, and the meaning of withholding them is that He does not return them to the world. ﴿And He releases the others until a specified term﴾, i.e., He releases the sleeping souls, and releasing them is returning them to the world. The specified term is the term of real death. People have spoken about the soul (nafs) and the spirit (ruh) and have greatly multiplied discussion on this by conjecture without verification. The correct view is that this is among the things whose knowledge Allah has kept to Himself, based on His saying: ﴿Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 43:

﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah?﴾ Here "am" (أم) means "bal" (بل, "rather"), and the hamzah is the hamzah of denunciation (همزة الإنكار). The intercessors (shufaʿa') are the idols and others, based on their saying: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18]. ﴿Say: "Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?"﴾ The interrogative hamzah has entered upon the waw of circumstance (واو الحال), its implied meaning being: "They intercede, while they possess nothing and do not understand."

Qur'an verse in parentheses with ﴿ ﴾ markers; translate meaning inside.

﴿Say: "To Allah belongs all intercession."﴾ That is, He is its owner, so no one may intercede with Him except by His permission. In this there is a refutation of the disbelievers in their claim that the idols intercede for them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 45:

﴿When Allah alone is mentioned, their hearts shrink in aversion﴾ (the verse). Its meaning is that the disbelievers dislike the tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness) and love to associate partners with Him. The meaning of ﴿shrink﴾ is that they contract out of intense aversion. It is narrated that this verse was revealed when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Surah al-Najm, and Satan cast into his recitation (umniyyah) as we mentioned in al-Hajj. The disbelievers rejoiced at what Satan had cast, namely the glorification of al-Lat and al-Uzza. Then, when Allah removed what Satan had cast, they became arrogant and recoiled.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 47:

﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been reckoning.﴾ That is, there will become manifest to them on the Day of Resurrection the opposite of what they used to think, because they used to entertain false assumptions. Al-Zamakhshari said: The purpose of this is to magnify the punishment that will befall them; that is, there will appear to them from the punishment of Allah what had not been within their calculation. It is like His saying regarding the reward: ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17]. It has also been said: its meaning is that they did deeds which they reckoned to be good deeds, but then they turned out to be evil deeds. Al-Hasan said: "Woe to the people of usury because of this verse." This is on the understanding that it refers to Muslims, while the apparent meaning is that it refers to disbelievers.

﴿And there befell them that which they used to mock.﴾ The meaning of *ḥāqa* (حاق) is "to descend upon, alight, and come down." Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others said: this is with an elision of a modifying noun (*ḥadhf muḍāf*), its intended meaning being: "There befell them the recompense of that which they used to mock." It is possible that the statement is without elision, and this is better. Its meaning is: "There befell them the recompense of that which they used to mock, because in the world they used to mock when they were warned of God's punishment, and they would say, 'When is this promise?'"

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verses 49–50:

﴿He said, "I was only given it on [the basis of] knowledge."﴾ It may bear two meanings. The first, which is the more apparent, is that he means "on knowledge from me of the means of gain and benefits." The second is "on Allah's knowledge of my deservingness of that." Here, "innamā" may bear two meanings. The first, which is the more apparent, is that "mā" is a kafffa (a particle that "restrains" the governing force of the verb, i.e., it turns innamā into a restrictive particle), and ﴿on knowledge﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The second is that "mā" is the subject of inna and ﴿on knowledge﴾ is its predicate. He said "ūtītuhu" with the masculine pronoun, though it refers to the blessing, in accordance with the sense (al-ḥaml ʿalā al-maʿnā). ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾: this is a rebuttal of the one who said "I was only given it on knowledge." ﴿Those before them already said it﴾: meaning Qarun and others.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verses 49–50:

﴿He said, "I was only given it on [the basis of] knowledge."﴾ It may bear two meanings. The first, which is the more apparent, is that he means "on knowledge from me of the means of gain and benefits." The second is "on Allah's knowledge of my deservingness of that." Here, "innamā" may bear two meanings. The first, which is the more apparent, is that "mā" is a kafffa (a particle that "restrains" the governing force of the verb, i.e., it turns innamā into a restrictive particle), and ﴿on knowledge﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The second is that "mā" is the subject of inna and ﴿on knowledge﴾ is its predicate. He said "ūtītuhu" with the masculine pronoun, though it refers to the blessing, in accordance with the sense (al-ḥaml ʿalā al-maʿnā). ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾: this is a rebuttal of the one who said "I was only given it on knowledge." ﴿Those before them already said it﴾: meaning Qarun and others.

Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Mas'ud said: "This is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an." It is also narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I would not love to have the world and all that is in it in exchange for this verse." Scholars differed about its occasion of revelation. It was said that it was revealed concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza, when he wished to embrace Islam but feared that God would not forgive him for what he had done in killing Hamza. It was also said that it was revealed concerning a people who believed but did not emigrate, were tested and fell into temptation, then regretted and thought they had no repentance. This is the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who wrote this verse to Hisham ibn al-As when this happened to him. It was further said that it was revealed concerning some people from the time of pre-Islamic ignorance (jahiliyya) who said, "Islam will not benefit us, for we have committed adultery and killed souls," so the verse was revealed concerning them. Its meaning, nevertheless, is general for all people until the Day of Resurrection, with a detailed explanation that we will mention. Those who "have transgressed against themselves" are either the disbelievers or the disobedient Muslims. If the intended meaning is the disbelievers, then the community (ummah) has agreed that when they embrace Islam, their disbelief and all their sins are forgiven, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Islam wipes out what came before it." And they agreed that if they die in disbelief, God will not forgive them but will make them abide forever in the Fire. If the intended meaning is the disobedient Muslims, then whoever disobeys and repents, God forgives his sins; and if he does not repent, he is subject to the will of God: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him. Thus the forgiveness mentioned in this verse may refer to the forgiveness of disbelievers when they embrace Islam, or to the forgiveness of disobedient believers when they repent, or to the forgiveness of disobedient believers even if they do not repent, when God graciously forgives them. The apparent meaning is that it was revealed concerning the disbelievers, and that the forgiveness mentioned is for them when they embrace Islam. The evidence that it concerns the disbelievers is what follows it, up to His words: ﴿Indeed, My verses came to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers.﴾ [Az-Zumar: 59].

Quranic quotations are in ﴿ ﴾. Translate.

﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. He means: follow the Qur'an. It is not that some parts of the Qur'an are better than others, for all of it is good. Rather the meaning is that they should follow in their deeds what it contains of commands, and avoid what it contains of prohibitions. So the comparative sense implied by "best" (aḥsan) lies in the following (al-ittibāʿ). It has been said that it means the abrogating (nāsikh) verses rather than the abrogated (mansūkh) ones, but this is far-fetched.

The object of purpose: its implied sense is "out of aversion that a soul should say." The soul is mentioned in indefinite form because what is meant is some souls, namely the souls of the disbelievers. ﴿In the side of Allah﴾ means in regard to Allah's right. It is also said to mean in the matter of Allah. Its origin is from *janb*, meaning side, and then it was used metaphorically (*istiʿāra*) in this sense. ﴿The mockers﴾ means those who ridiculed. ﴿Balā﴾ (the particle meaning "yes indeed") is a reply to the soul whose speech was quoted. The particle *balā* is only used to answer a negative statement, and here it answers her words: ﴿If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing﴾, because this has the sense of a negation, since *law* (if only) is a particle of impossibility. The implied answer is: "Nay, indeed there has come to you guidance from Allah through His sending of messengers and His sending down of scriptures." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is a reply to her words ﴿If only I had a return﴾, since its meaning implies that the lifespan is wide enough for reflection, so it was said to him ﴿Balā﴾ as a rejection of that. The first view is more fitting to the context of the speech, because His words ﴿My signs had already come to you﴾ explain what *balā* contains. ﴿Their faces will be blackened﴾ may mean the literal darkness of color, or it may be a metaphor for severe distress. ﴿With their salvation﴾: its origin is from *fawz* (success), and the implied meaning is "because of their success." It is also said the meaning is "with their virtues." ﴿And He is over all things a Disposer﴾ means He is the one who manages every thing.

﴿Maqālīd﴾ means keys, and it is also said treasuries. Its singular is *iqlīd*. It is also said it has no singular from its own root, and that its origin is a Persian word. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the keys of the heavens and the earth, and he said: "They are: *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, *Allāhu akbar*, *subḥān Allāh*, *al-ḥamdu lillāh*, *lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh*, and *astaghfir Allāh*. He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden; in His hand is the good; He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things Powerful." If this hadith is authentic, its meaning is that whoever says these words sincerely and truthfully attains the good things and blessings from the heavens and the earth, because these words lead to that, so they are as if they were keys to it. ﴿And those who disbelieved﴾ and the verse that follows: al-Zamakhsharī said: it is connected to His words ﴿And Allah will deliver those who feared Him with their success﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (*iʿtirāḍ*).

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 64:

﴿Afa-ghayra Allah﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "a'budu" (I worship). ﴿Ta'murunni﴾: one of the two nuns has been dropped for lightness (takhfif), and it is also read with the one nun assimilated into the other (idgham).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 65:

﴿If you associate (others with Allah), your deeds will surely be nullified.﴾ This is evidence that the deeds of an apostate are nullified absolutely, contrary to al-Shafi'i's view, in his statement: "His deeds are not nullified unless he dies in disbelief." If it is said: those who were revealed to were a group, yet the address in ﴿If you associate (others with Allah)﴾ is in the singular. The answer is that it was revealed to each one of them individually. If it is said: how were the prophets addressed with this, when they are protected (ma'sum) from associating partners with Allah? The answer is that it is by way of supposition and hypothesis, i.e., if association had occurred from them, their deeds would have been nullified; but association did not occur from them, owing to their protection ('isma). It is also possible that the address was directed to others, and the prophets were addressed so that the meaning would indicate others by a stronger inference (al-tariq al-awla).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 67:

﴿And they did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾. That is, they did not glorify Him with the glorification due to Him, nor did they describe Him with what is incumbent upon Him, nor did they declare Him free of what is not befitting to Him. The pronoun in "qadaru" refers to the Quraysh, and it was said: to the Jews. ﴿And the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾. The purpose of this is to magnify the majesty of Allah and to refute the disbelievers who did not measure Allah with His true measure. Then people differed concerning it, as they differed concerning other ambiguous matters. The interpreters (al-mata'awwilah) said: the handful and the right hand are an expression for power. Ibn al-Tayyib said: they are an attribute additional to the attributes of the Essence. As for the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih), they entrusted the knowledge of this to Allah, and regarded it as among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters whose true reality none knows except Allah. Ibn 'Abbas has said, in substance: the earth is in His handful and the heavens are folded up, all of it by His right hand. Ibn 'Umar has said, in substance: the earth is in the one handful, and the heavens are folded up in the other hand, the right hand, because both of His hands are right hands.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verse 68:

﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾ It is the horn into which Israfil (Israfil) blows. This blast is the blast of swooning (nafkhat al-sa'q), which is death. It has been said that before it there is the blast of terror (nafkhat al-fazaʿ), which is not mentioned in this verse. ﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾ It has been said: meaning Jibril and Israfil, and Mikail and the Angel of Death. Then Allah causes them to die after that. It has also been said: the exception refers to the prophets. And it has been said: the martyrs. ﴿Then it will be blown again﴾ This is the blast of rising (nafkhat al-qiyam), ﴿and behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾. It is from "looking" (al-nazar). It has also been said: it is from "waiting" (al-intizar), meaning they will be waiting to see what will be done to them.

The Book will be placed, meaning the books of deeds; he used the singular because he intends the genus. It is also said that it is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz).

﴿And the prophets will be brought forth﴾ to bear witness against their peoples, ﴿and the witnesses﴾. This may be the plural of witness (shahid) or the plural of martyr (shahid) who fell in the way of Allah. The first is more preferred, because it carries the sense of warning (wa'id), and because it is more fitting alongside the mention of the prophets as witnesses. The intended meaning according to this view is the Community of Muhammad (ﷺ), since they bear witness over people. It is also said: it means the guardian angels (al-hafaza al-malaika).

﴿And judgment will be passed between them﴾: the pronoun refers to all of creation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 39, verses 71–75:

﴿زُمَراً﴾ (zumaran, "in groups"): in both places it is the plural of zumra (zumrah), meaning a group of people. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first group to enter Paradise will have faces like the moon on the night of the full moon, and the second group will be like the brightest star in the sky in its radiance. Then after that they will be in (different) ranks."

﴿خَزَنَتُهَآ﴾ (khazanatuha, "its keepers"): the plural of khazin (keeper), wherever it occurs. ﴿كَلِمَةُ ٱلْعَذَابِ﴾ (kalimat al-'adhab, "the word of punishment"): meaning the prior decree concerning their punishment. ﴿فُتِحَتْ أَبْوَابُهَا﴾ (futihat abwabuha, "its gates were opened"): He said regarding Paradise "and its gates were opened" with the waw (wa), and regarding Hell "were opened" without the waw, because the gates of Paradise were already open before its people arrived. The meaning is: until, when they come to it while its gates are already open. So the waw is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the answer to "idha" (when) in this case is omitted. As for the gates of Hell, they were opened when they came to it, so the phrase "were opened" is the answer to the conditional, as if it were without a waw. The Kufans said: the waw in "its gates" (of Paradise) is the waw of the eight (waw al-thamaniya), because the gates of Paradise are eight. It was also said: the waw is extra, and "futihat" is the answer.

﴿وَأَوْرَثَنَا ٱلأَرْضَ﴾ (wa-awrathana al-ard, "and He has caused us to inherit the earth"): meaning the land of Paradise. The inheritance here is a metaphor, as if they inherited the place of those who did not enter Paradise. ﴿نَتَبَوَّأُ﴾ (natabawwa'u, "we may settle"): that is, we may dwell in Paradise wherever we wish and take it as a dwelling. ﴿حَآفِّينَ مِنْ حَوْلِ ٱلْعَرْشِ﴾ (hafifin min hawl al-'arsh, "circling around the Throne"): that is, surrounding it and moving around it. ﴿وَقُضِيَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ (wa-qudiya baynahum, "and judgment will be passed between them"): the pronoun refers to all of creation, as in the first place; it may also here refer to the angels, and the judgment between them is the full payment of their rewards according to their ranks. ﴿وَقِيلَ ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ (wa-qila al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin, "and it will be said: Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds"): the one who says this may be the angels, or all of creation, or the people of Paradise, based on His saying: ﴿وَآخِرُ دَعْوَاهُمْ أَنِ ٱلْحَمْدُ للَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ "And their last call will be: Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (Yunus 10:10).

﴿خَزَنَتُهَآ﴾ (khazanatuha, "its keepers"): the plural of khazin (keeper), wherever it occurs. ﴿كَلِمَةُ ٱلْعَذَابِ﴾ (kalimat al-'adhab, "the word of punishment"): meaning the prior decree concerning their punishment. ﴿فُتِحَتْ أَبْوَابُهَا﴾ (futihat abwabuha, "its gates were opened"): He said regarding Paradise "and its gates were opened" with the waw (wa), and regarding Hell "were opened" without the waw, because the gates of Paradise were already open before its people arrived. The meaning is: until, when they come to it while its gates are already open. So the waw is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the answer to "idha" (when) in this case is omitted. As for the gates of Hell, they were opened when they came to it, so the phrase "were opened" is the answer to the conditional, as if it were without a waw. The Kufans said: the waw in "its gates" (of Paradise) is the waw of the eight (waw al-thamaniya), because the gates of Paradise are eight. It was also said: the waw is extra, and "futihat" is the answer.

﴿وَأَوْرَثَنَا ٱلأَرْضَ﴾ (wa-awrathana al-ard, "and He has caused us to inherit the earth"): meaning the land of Paradise. The inheritance here is a metaphor, as if they inherited the place of those who did not enter Paradise. ﴿نَتَبَوَّأُ﴾ (natabawwa'u, "we may settle"): that is, we may dwell in Paradise wherever we wish and take it as a dwelling. ﴿حَآفِّينَ مِنْ حَوْلِ ٱلْعَرْشِ﴾ (hafifin min hawl al-'arsh, "circling around the Throne"): that is, surrounding it and moving around it. ﴿وَقُضِيَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ (wa-qudiya baynahum, "and judgment will be passed between them"): the pronoun refers to all of creation, as in the first place; it may also here refer to the angels, and the judgment between them is the full payment of their rewards according to their ranks. ﴿وَقِيلَ ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ (wa-qila al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin, "and it will be said: Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds"): the one who says this may be the angels, or all of creation, or the people of Paradise, based on His saying: ﴿وَآخِرُ دَعْوَاهُمْ أَنِ ٱلْحَمْدُ للَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ "And their last call will be: Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (Yunus 10:10).
